claim: Cellular senescence was previously identified as a process that permanently halts the proliferation of normal cells in culture following replicative exhaustion.
source: Cellular senescence was previously identified as a process that permanently halts the proliferation of normal cells in culture following replicative exhaustion (Hayflick and Moorhead, 1961).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hayflick and Moorhead, 1961

claim: Cellular senescence is a stress response that acts both in culture and in vivo to prevent proliferation of cells exposed to oncogenic stress.
source: It subsequently became clear that cellular senescence is a stress response that acts both in culture and in vivo to prevent proliferation of cells exposed to oncogenic stress, such as telomere attrition, and various types of DNA damage and oncogene insertions (Serrano et al., 1997; Bodnar et al., 1998; d'Adda di Fagagna, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Serrano et al., 1997; Bodnar et al., 1998; d'Adda di Fagagna, 2008

claim: Cellular senescence acts as an effective anti-tumourigenic mechanism.
source: It therefore acts as an effective anti-tumourigenic mechanism (Braig et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005; Collado et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braig et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005; Collado et al., 2005

claim: Long-term accumulation of senescent cells leads to disruption of tissue structure and function.
source: However, senescent cells can also have detrimental effects on biological processes. Long-term accumulation of senescent cells leads to disruption of tissue structure and function, possibly through the acquisition of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (Campisi, 2005; Campisi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campisi, 2005; Campisi et al., 2011

claim: In most species there is a marked accumulation of senescent cells with time.
source: This is particularly relevant in the context of ageing, as in most species there is a marked accumulation of senescent cells with time (Herbig et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009; van Deursen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herbig et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009; van Deursen, 2014

claim: There is a causative link between cellular senescence and age-related deterioration.
source: Indeed, recent studies have uncovered a causative link between cellular senescence and age-related deterioration (Baker et al., 2008, 2011, 2013), underscoring the therapeutic benefits of targeting senescent cells (Naylor et al., 2013; van Deursen, 2014), and establishing cellular senescence as a hallmark of ageing (Lopez-Otin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker et al., 2008, 2011, 2013

claim: In mammals, the ability to regenerate tissues declines with age.
source: In mammals, the ability to regenerate tissues declines with age (Sousa-Victor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sousa-Victor et al., 2014

claim: The decline in muscle regeneration with age has been linked to the loss of quiescent stem cells through senescence.
source: The decline in muscle regeneration with age has recently been linked to the loss of quiescent stem cells through senescence (Sousa-Victor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sousa-Victor et al., 2014

claim: Zebrafish and salamanders are able to accomplish perfect regeneration of a wide range of complex structures throughout their lifespan.
source: In contrast, other vertebrates, such as zebrafish and salamanders, are able to accomplish perfect regeneration of a wide range of complex structures throughout their lifespan (Margotta et al., 2002; Azevedo et al., 2011; Eguchi et al., 2011; Itou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Margotta et al., 2002; Azevedo et al., 2011; Eguchi et al., 2011; Itou et al., 2012

claim: Up to 80% of UV-irradiated salamander cells entered a state of cell cycle withdrawal within 12 days.
source: Up to 80% of the irradiated cells entered a state of cell cycle withdrawal within 12 days that, in contrast to quiescence, was accompanied by high levels of Gadd45 expression, permanent γH2AX foci, and high levels of senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-βgal), a hallmark of cellular senescence (Dimri et al., 1995; Campisi, 2011) (Figure 1B–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-F and citations to Dimri et al., 1995; Campisi, 2011

claim: The timing of SA-βgal induction in salamander cells is similar to that reported in mammalian fibroblasts undergoing stress-induced senescence.
source: The timing of SA-βgal induction in salamander cells is similar to that reported in mammalian fibroblasts undergoing stress-induced senescence (Parrinello et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parrinello et al., 2003

claim: SA-βgal positive A1 cells do not re-enter the cell cycle upon serum stimulation.
source: While proliferating or quiescent A1 cells re-enter the cell cycle upon serum stimulation (indicated by the incorporation of the nucleotide analogue EdU), SA-βgal positive A1 cells do not, as demonstrated by double SA-βgal/Edu staining (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Senescent salamander cells exhibit sustained production of reactive oxygen species.
source: Furthermore, the cells identified by the SA-βgal staining exhibit other markers of senescence (Campisi, 2005) such as sustained production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and extended mitochondrial and lysosomal networks (Figure 1F,H) relative to non-senescent parallel cultures.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,H and citation to Campisi, 2005

claim: Senescent salamander cells acquire a secretory phenotype comprising cytokines, signalling and matrix remodelling factors.
source: In addition, these cells acquire a secretory phenotype comprising a number of cytokines, signalling and matrix remodelling factors (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Many factors in the senescent salamander cell secretory phenotype have been previously reported to integrate the senescence-associated phenotype (SASP) in various contexts of mammalian senescence.
source: It is nothworthy that many of these factors, such as the interleukins IL-1a, IL-1b, IL-13, IL-7, IFNγ (Interferon gamma), TNF-α (Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha), M-CSF (Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor), the matrix metelloproteases MMP1, 3 and 9, uPA (urokinase-type Plasminogen Activator) and Cathepsin D, have been previously reported to integrate the senescence-associated phenotype (SASP) in various contexts of mammalian senescence (Coppé et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppé et al., 2010

claim: The regulation and properties of the senescent state are comparable in salamanders and mammals.
source: Together, these data suggest that the regulation and properties of the senescent state are comparable in salamanders and mammals.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: There is a significant induction of cellular senescence during the intermediate stages of salamander limb regeneration (mid-blastema and palette).
source: We found that there is a significant induction of cellular senescence during the intermediate stages of regeneration (mid-blastema and palette), but that the number of senescent cells diminishes subsequently (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: The number of senescent cells diminishes after the intermediate stages of salamander limb regeneration.
source: We found that there is a significant induction of cellular senescence during the intermediate stages of regeneration (mid-blastema and palette), but that the number of senescent cells diminishes subsequently (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: Within the regenerating limb, senescent cells are found at the level of the amputation plane, including cartilage and muscle, and within the blastema.
source: Within the regenerating limb, senescent cells are found at the level of the amputation plane, including cartilage and muscle, and within the blastema, including fibroblast, monocyte-like cells, and epidermal glands (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: No SA-βgal+/EdU+ cells were detected in regenerating or normal salamander tissues following systemic EdU injections.
source: To corroborate that SA-βgal+ cells exhibit other hallmarks of cellular senescence in vivo, we performed SA-βgal/EdU stainings in regenerating or normal tissues following systemic EdU injections. We were unable to detect SA-βgal+/EdU+ cells under any condition examined (Figure 2C), suggesting that SA-βgal+ cells are withdrawn from the cell cycle, a characteristic of senescent cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: SA-βgal+ cells in salamander tissues are withdrawn from the cell cycle.
source: We were unable to detect SA-βgal+/EdU+ cells under any condition examined (Figure 2C), suggesting that SA-βgal+ cells are withdrawn from the cell cycle, a characteristic of senescent cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Induction and disappearance of senescent cells occur during axolotl limb regeneration.
source: Similar observations were made in another salamander species, the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum), both in mature animals as well as at early stages of development (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E

claim: No significant induction of senescence takes place during normal salamander limb development.
source: Interestingly, the induction and subsequent disappearance of senescent cells appear to be characteristic of regeneration, as no significant induction of senescence takes place during normal limb development (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in contrast to previous findings in amniotic limb development (Banito and Lowe, 2013; Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations to Banito and Lowe, 2013; Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013

claim: The induction and subsequent disappearance of senescent cells appear to be characteristic of regeneration in salamanders.
source: Interestingly, the induction and subsequent disappearance of senescent cells appear to be characteristic of regeneration, as no significant induction of senescence takes place during normal limb development (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in contrast to previous findings in amniotic limb development (Banito and Lowe, 2013; Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Cellular senescence is a normal process during salamander limb regeneration and is subject to dynamic regulation.
source: These observations suggest that cellular senescence is a normal process during salamander limb regeneration, and is subject to dynamic regulation.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2

claim: Salamanders have the ability to undergo multiple rounds of regeneration through their lives.
source: Salamanders have the remarkable ability to undergo multiple rounds of regeneration through their lives (Eguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eguchi et al., 2011

claim: The percentage of senescent cells does not increase following sequential amputation–regeneration cycles in salamanders.
source: However, we found that the percentage of senescent cells does not increase following sequential amputation–regeneration cycles. The tissues of adult newts that had been subjected to five regeneration cycles over 1.5 years did not show any accumulation of senescent cells compared to intact limbs (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Elimination of senescent cells occurs during each round of limb regeneration in salamanders.
source: This data suggests that elimination of senescent cells occurs during each round of limb regeneration.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The proportion of senescent cells within tissues increases as the organism matures in most species studied so far, including mammals.
source: The proportion of senescent cells within tissues is known to increase as the organism matures in most species studied so far, including mammals (Herbig et al., 2006; van Deursen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herbig et al., 2006; van Deursen, 2014

claim: The percentage of senescent cells in heart, spleen and liver does not increase in older salamanders.
source: Remarkably, we found that the percentage of senescent cells in heart, spleen and liver does not increase in older salamanders (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3); the latter two organs are known to accumulate senescent cells in mammals as they age (Herbig et al., 2006; van Deursen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citations to Herbig et al., 2006; van Deursen, 2014

claim: Spleen and liver are known to accumulate senescent cells in mammals as they age.
source: Remarkably, we found that the percentage of senescent cells in heart, spleen and liver does not increase in older salamanders (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3); the latter two organs are known to accumulate senescent cells in mammals as they age (Herbig et al., 2006; van Deursen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herbig et al., 2006; van Deursen, 2014

claim: Active mechanisms of senescent cell clearance operate within normal and regenerating salamander tissues.
source: Together, these findings raise the possibility that active mechanisms of senescent cell clearance operate within normal and regenerating salamander tissues.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2F, 2G

claim: Normal salamander cells persist for at least 40 days after implantation within newt limb tissues.
source: After an initial non-specific loss of cells following implantation, the normal cells (A1 GFP+) persist for at least 40 days and contribute to structures within the limb tissues (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: 80% of the implanted senescent cell population is cleared from salamander limb tissues within 2 weeks post-implantation.
source: In contrast, 80% of the implanted senescent cell population is cleared from the limb tissues within 2 weeks post-implantation (Figure 3A,B), consistent with a half-life of 9 days (calculated from the exponential equation corresponding to the senescent dataset, after subtraction of the initial loss observed in normal cells), comparable to the rate of clearance of senescent cells during regeneration (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 2

claim: The half-life of implanted senescent cells in salamander limb tissues is 9 days.
source: In contrast, 80% of the implanted senescent cell population is cleared from the limb tissues within 2 weeks post-implantation (Figure 3A,B), consistent with a half-life of 9 days (calculated from the exponential equation corresponding to the senescent dataset, after subtraction of the initial loss observed in normal cells), comparable to the rate of clearance of senescent cells during regeneration (Figure 2).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: The rate of clearance of nGFP+ senescent cells corresponds to the rate of clearance of unlabelled senescent cells in salamander tissues.
source: To distinguish between these two possibilities, we performed the same experiment using retrovirally labelled nGFP senescent cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The rate of clearance of nGFP+ senescent cells corresponds to the rate of clearance of unlabelled senescent cells, supporting the clearance hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Salamander tissues have a significant capacity for senescent cell clearance.
source: These data suggest that salamander tissues have a significant capacity for senescent cell clearance.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Implantation of a 1:1 mixture of senescent and normal cells results in the clearance of both populations in salamander tissues.
source: Interestingly, the implantation of a 1:1 mixture of senescent and normal cells does not result in the persistence of the normal cells, but in the clearance of both populations (Figure 3B, Figure 4A,B), albeit with a delay when compared to the clearance of purely senescent cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 4A,B

claim: Senescent cells are able to induce senescence in their neighbours, a phenomenon termed 'senescence bystander effect'.
source: It has been recently shown that senescent cells are able to induce senescence in their neighbours, a phenomenon termed 'senescence bystander effect' (Nelson et al., 2012; Acosta et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nelson et al., 2012; Acosta et al., 2013

claim: Cellular senescence can be induced in normal salamander cells by co-culture with senescent cells.
source: We found that this property is also present in senescent salamander cells. Cellular senescence can be induced in normal cells by co-culture with senescent cells (Figure 4C), or following incubation with purified media from senescent populations (Figure 4D), supporting the idea that senescence can be transmitted in a paracrine fashion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Cellular senescence can be induced in normal salamander cells following incubation with purified media from senescent populations.
source: Cellular senescence can be induced in normal cells by co-culture with senescent cells (Figure 4C), or following incubation with purified media from senescent populations (Figure 4D), supporting the idea that senescence can be transmitted in a paracrine fashion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Senescence can be transmitted in a paracrine fashion in salamander cells.
source: Cellular senescence can be induced in normal cells by co-culture with senescent cells (Figure 4C), or following incubation with purified media from senescent populations (Figure 4D), supporting the idea that senescence can be transmitted in a paracrine fashion.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Implantation of a 1:1 mixture of senescent and normal cells results in the induction of senescence in normal cells in salamander tissues.
source: In addition, implantation of the 1:1 mixture of senescent + normal cells results in the induction of senescence in normal cells (Figure 4E,F), providing an explanation for their eventual clearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: Active mechanisms identify and target senescent cells for clearance within salamander tissues.
source: Together, these results suggest that active mechanisms identify and target senescent cells for clearance within salamander tissues.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: The immune system plays a role in the surveillance and clearance of p53 or oncogene-induced senescent hepatocytes in mice.
source: A series of elegant experiments have recently described a role for the immune system in the surveillance and clearance of p53 or oncogene-induced senescent hepatocytes in mice (Xue et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2011; Lujambio et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xue et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2011; Lujambio et al., 2013

claim: There is an extensive recruitment of immune cells, and in particular macrophages, to the regenerating limb in salamanders.
source: In addition, recent evidence suggests that there is an extensive recruitment of immune cells, and in particular macrophages, to the regenerating limb in salamanders (Godwin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Godwin et al., 2013

claim: TMR-dextran is specifically internalised by macrophages in salamanders.
source: In vivo labelling using TMR-dextran, which is specifically internalised by macrophages (Figure 5A–C), as well as monocyte specific α-naphthyl acetate esterase staining (Figure 5D), reveal that macrophages and senescent cells are found in close proximity within regenerating limbs, suggesting cell-to-cell contact and engulfment in some cases.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C

claim: Macrophages and senescent cells are found in close proximity within regenerating salamander limbs.
source: In vivo labelling using TMR-dextran, which is specifically internalised by macrophages (Figure 5A–C), as well as monocyte specific α-naphthyl acetate esterase staining (Figure 5D), reveal that macrophages and senescent cells are found in close proximity within regenerating limbs, suggesting cell-to-cell contact and engulfment in some cases.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–D

claim: Treatment with clodrosomes is able to reduce the macrophage population by fivefold in salamanders.
source: We found that treatment with clodrosomes is able to reduce the macrophage population by fivefold, compared with control DiI liposomes (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Clodronate-filled liposomes are specifically internalised by macrophages in salamanders.
source: As with the TMR-dextran, these liposomes are specifically internalised by macrophages, as shown by their incorporation into cells expressing F4/80, a specific macrophage marker (Morris et al., 1991) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and citation to Morris et al., 1991

claim: At 20 hr post implantation, there is a strong accumulation of DiI-labelled macrophages in the vicinity of senescent cells in salamander regenerating limbs.
source: At 20 hr post implantation, we observed a strong accumulation of DiI-labelled macrophages in the vicinity of senescent cells (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–F

claim: Macrophage recruitment to areas of normal cells is not significantly different from their recruitment to other areas of the limb mesenchyme.
source: In contrast, macrophage recruitment to areas of normal cells (control) was not significantly different from their recruitment to other areas of the limb mesenchyme (Figure 6D,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,F

claim: Senescent cells are cleared in animals injected with control DiI liposomes but remain in animals whose macrophages had been depleted.
source: At 2 weeks post implantation, the normal cells remained within the regenerating limbs (Figure 6G). However, the senescent cells were cleared in animals injected with control DiI liposomes, but remained in animals whose macrophages had been depleted (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: The macrophage is critical for clearance of senescent cells in salamanders.
source: This demonstrates that the macrophage is critical for clearance of senescent cells, and constitutes the first evidence for senescence surveillance mechanisms that operate during normal regeneration.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: This study constitutes the first evidence for senescence surveillance mechanisms that operate during normal regeneration.
source: This demonstrates that the macrophage is critical for clearance of senescent cells, and constitutes the first evidence for senescence surveillance mechanisms that operate during normal regeneration.
evidence: Based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript

claim: Salamanders possess a rapid and efficient mechanism to recognise and clear senescent cells that either arise endogenously, or are introduced from culture.
source: It is clear that salamanders possess a rapid and efficient mechanism to recognise and clear senescent cells that either arise endogenously, or are introduced from culture.
evidence: Based on inference from all experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A robust macrophage-dependent surveillance mechanism operates in normal and regenerating tissues of adult salamanders.
source: Our study demonstrates that a robust macrophage-dependent surveillance mechanism operates in normal and regenerating tissues of adult salamanders, and this allows them to circumvent the negative effects associated with the long-term accumulation of senescent cells, such as the disruption of tissue structure and function (Campisi, 2005; Rodier and Campisi, 2011).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and citations to Campisi, 2005; Rodier and Campisi, 2011

claim: Macrophage-dependent surveillance mechanisms allow salamanders to circumvent the negative effects associated with the long-term accumulation of senescent cells.
source: Our study demonstrates that a robust macrophage-dependent surveillance mechanism operates in normal and regenerating tissues of adult salamanders, and this allows them to circumvent the negative effects associated with the long-term accumulation of senescent cells, such as the disruption of tissue structure and function (Campisi, 2005; Rodier and Campisi, 2011).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and citations to Campisi, 2005; Rodier and Campisi, 2011

claim: There is a notable induction of cellular senescence during salamander limb regeneration.
source: These surveillance mechanisms are particularly significant for limb regeneration because there is a notable induction of cellular senescence during this process.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Systemic macrophage depletion during salamander limb regeneration leads to defects in this process.
source: Consistent with this, recent reports show that systemic macrophage depletion during salamander limb regeneration leads to defects in this process (Godwin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Godwin et al., 2013

claim: Macrophage depletion during zebrafish fin regeneration leads to defects in this process.
source: This has also been observed during zebrafish fin regeneration (Petrie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petrie et al., 2014

claim: Cellular senescence has been shown to contribute to the decline in muscle regenerative ability upon ageing in mammals.
source: Furthermore, cellular senescence has been recently shown to contribute to the decline in muscle regenerative ability upon ageing in mammals (Wang et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2011; Sousa-Victor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2011; Sousa-Victor et al., 2014

claim: The effective immune clearance of senescent cells in salamanders supports their ability to undergo multiple rounds of regeneration through their lifespan.
source: In light of these observations, we propose that the effective immune clearance of senescent cells in salamanders supports their ability to undergo multiple rounds of regeneration through their lifespan (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on inference from all experimental data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 7

claim: Senescent cells could play a positive role during regeneration.
source: Nevertheless, it is interesting that we find a consistent induction of cellular senescence during regeneration, suggesting that this could be integral to the mechanism. Senescent cells could play a positive role during regeneration, a proposal that is consistent with recent findings that senescence contributes to tissue remodelling during mouse development (Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013; Campisi, 2014) and wound healing (Krizhanovsky et al., 2008; Jun and Lau, 2010; Demaria et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013; Campisi, 2014; Krizhanovsky et al., 2008; Jun and Lau, 2010; Demaria et al., 2014

claim: Senescence contributes to tissue remodelling during mouse development.
source: Senescent cells could play a positive role during regeneration, a proposal that is consistent with recent findings that senescence contributes to tissue remodelling during mouse development (Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013; Campisi, 2014) and wound healing (Krizhanovsky et al., 2008; Jun and Lau, 2010; Demaria et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013; Campisi, 2014

claim: Senescence contributes to wound healing.
source: Senescent cells could play a positive role during regeneration, a proposal that is consistent with recent findings that senescence contributes to tissue remodelling during mouse development (Munoz-Espin et al., 2013; Storer et al., 2013; Campisi, 2014) and wound healing (Krizhanovsky et al., 2008; Jun and Lau, 2010; Demaria et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krizhanovsky et al., 2008; Jun and Lau, 2010; Demaria et al., 2014

claim: Senescent cells could contribute to regeneration indirectly, by promoting the efficient recruitment of macrophages.
source: Alternatively, senescent cells could contribute to regeneration indirectly, by promoting the efficient recruitment of macrophages, since the latter have been shown to promote tissue remodelling and patterning in various contexts, including regeneration (Lobov et al., 2005; Qian and Pollard, 2012; Petrie et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to Lobov et al., 2005; Qian and Pollard, 2012; Petrie et al., 2014

claim: Macrophages have been shown to promote tissue remodelling and patterning in various contexts, including regeneration.
source: Alternatively, senescent cells could contribute to regeneration indirectly, by promoting the efficient recruitment of macrophages, since the latter have been shown to promote tissue remodelling and patterning in various contexts, including regeneration (Lobov et al., 2005; Qian and Pollard, 2012; Petrie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lobov et al., 2005; Qian and Pollard, 2012; Petrie et al., 2014

claim: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype is likely to play an important role in regeneration.
source: In either case, the senescence-associated secretory phenotype is likely to play an important role.
evidence: Based on speculation from the experimental findings

claim: Targeting senescent cells could lead to therapeutic strategies for age-related pathologies.
source: It has recently been suggested that targeting senescent cells could lead to therapeutic strategies for age-related pathologies (Naylor et al., 2013; van Deursen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Naylor et al., 2013; van Deursen, 2014

claim: Analysis of the salamander senescent cell surveillance mechanism could lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets for the amelioration of age-related disorders and extension of healthspan.
source: Here, we identify an animal with an efficient mechanism for surveillance of senescent cells operating through adulthood. Analysis of this mechanism could lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets for the amelioration of age-related disorders and extension of healthspan.
evidence: Based on speculation from the experimental findings

claim: Procedures for care and manipulation of all animals used in this study were performed in compliance with the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986, approved by the United Kingdom Home Office.
source: Procedures for care and manipulation of all animals used in this study were performed in compliance with the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986, approved by the United Kingdom Home Office.
evidence: Statement of regulatory compliance

claim: F4/80 is a specific macrophage marker.
source: As with the TMR-dextran, these liposomes are specifically internalised by macrophages, as shown by their incorporation into cells expressing F4/80, a specific macrophage marker (Morris et al., 1991) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morris et al., 1991

claim: Clodronate salt-filled liposomes are internalised specifically by macrophages via phagocytosis.
source: To determine whether macrophages mediate the clearance of senescent cells, we took advantage of an efficient method for macrophage depletion, based on the intravenous administration of selectively toxic, clodronate salt-filled liposomes (clodrosomes). These are internalised specifically by macrophages via phagocytosis (van Rooijen and Hendrikx, 2010) and have been shown to operate effectively in salamanders (Godwin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Rooijen and Hendrikx, 2010; Godwin et al., 2013

claim: Clodronate-filled liposomes have been shown to operate effectively in salamanders.
source: These are internalised specifically by macrophages via phagocytosis (van Rooijen and Hendrikx, 2010) and have been shown to operate effectively in salamanders (Godwin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Godwin et al., 2013
